title: The log folder that filled up
story: A small log volume is mounted at /var/log/app. It is full, so the app cannot write. A background process called app-writer must keep running and keep writing heartbeat.log.
goals: Free the log volume so it is under 50 percent full.
Keep app-writer running.
Keep heartbeat.log and leave the volume mounted.
hints: Run df -h to see which volume is full.
Run ls -lh /var/log/app and see which files are large.
You may delete or empty the big log. Emptying with : > file keeps the file in place.

title: Full disk with nothing to delete
story: The volume at /var/data is almost full, but ls shows no big file. A process called ingest deleted its queue file while still holding it open, so the space is not returned.
goals: Get /var/data under 60 percent full.
Keep the ingest process running (restart it if you must).
hints: du -sh /var/data shows little, but df -h shows it is full. Why would they differ?
A deleted file stays on disk while a process keeps it open. Look in /proc/PID/fd.
Run ls -l /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep deleted.
You can truncate through the descriptor, or stop the process and start it again.
solution:
ps | grep ingest
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | grep deleted
: > /proc/<pid>/fd/3
# or: kill <pid> and run /usr/local/bin/ingest again
df -h /var/data

title: The deploy user cannot run the release script
story: The user deploy must run /srv/app/run.sh, but it fails. The directory and the file are both owned by root.
goals: Let the deploy user run /srv/app/run.sh.
Do not make the file or the folder writable by everyone.
hints: Try it: su -s /bin/sh deploy -c /srv/app/run.sh
ls -ld /srv/app and ls -l /srv/app/run.sh show owner, group and mode.
A user needs execute on the directory to enter it, and execute plus read on a script to run it.

title: The job that eats the CPU
story: The machine feels slow. A runaway job started by report-job is burning CPU. A server called api-server must stay up.
goals: Stop report-job and everything it started.
Keep api-server running.
hints: Run top or ps to see the busy process.
Killing the busy process may not help if its parent starts it again.
Find the parent script, stop it first, then stop the child.
solution:
ps
kill $(pidof report-job)   # the parent loop first
kill $(pidof yes)
ps

title: The web server that will not start
story: start-web refuses to start the site. The settings file is /etc/web/web.conf and the site should answer on port 8080.
goals: Fix /etc/web/web.conf so PORT is 8080 and ROOT points to the real folder.
Start the server so http://127.0.0.1:8080/ answers.
hints: Run start-web and read the error message.
Compare PORT with a number: can you spot a letter?
ls /srv shows which folder really exists.

title: Port 8080 is taken
story: The new site must listen on port 8080, but an old web server still holds it. start-web starts the new one.
goals: Find and stop whatever holds port 8080.
Start the new site with start-web so port 8080 serves "MARGA web v2".
hints: netstat -tln lists the ports that are listening. Is 8080 one of them?
ps shows every process with its command line. Look for the one started with port 8080.
Stop that process, then run start-web.
solution:
netstat -tln | grep 8080
ps | grep httpd
kill <pid>
start-web
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

title: The pidfile that lies
story: start-web says the server is already running, but nothing answers on port 8080.
goals: Find out whether the process in the pidfile is really alive.
Start the server so it answers on port 8080 and leaves a valid pidfile.
hints: cat /run/web.pid shows the pid it remembers.
ls /proc/4242 or ps tells you if that pid is alive.
A pidfile for a dead process is stale and safe to remove.
solution:
cat /run/web.pid
ps | grep 4242
rm /run/web.pid
start-web
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

title: The host name that does not resolve
story: The tool db-check must find the address of db.internal. Name lookups use /etc/hosts here. The database is reachable at 127.0.0.2 in this lab.
goals: Make db-check report db.internal as 127.0.0.2.
Keep the localhost entry in /etc/hosts.
hints: Run db-check and read the message.
cat /etc/hosts shows what names are known. Compare the spelling with db.internal.
Add a line: address, then the name.

title: The release that points nowhere
story: /opt/app/current is a symlink to the active release, and it is broken. The newest release folder is under /opt/app/releases.
goals: Point /opt/app/current to the 2024-09 release.
Keep current as a symlink.
hints: ls -l /opt/app shows where current points.
ls /opt/app/releases shows which releases exist.
ln -sfn replaces a symlink in one step.

title: Who is causing the 502 errors?
story: /var/log/web/access.log is a web access log. Field 1 is the client address and field 9 is the status code. Find how many 502 responses there are and which client has the most.
goals: Write two lines to /root/answer.txt: count=NUMBER and ip=ADDRESS.
count is the number of lines with status 502. ip is the client with the most 502 lines.
hints: head -3 /var/log/web/access.log shows the fields.
awk '$9==502' keeps only the 502 lines.
Count with wc -l. For the busiest client use awk, sort, uniq -c and sort -rn.
solution:
awk '$9==502' /var/log/web/access.log | wc -l
awk '$9==502{print $1}' /var/log/web/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1
printf 'count=N\nip=ADDRESS\n' > /root/answer.txt

title: The backup script that lies
story: /usr/local/bin/backup.sh copies a folder to /backup. It breaks on folder names with a space, and it prints "backup finished OK" even when the source is missing.
goals: backup.sh "/srv/my data" must copy the folder and exit 0.
backup.sh /srv/missing must exit non-zero and must not print "finished OK".
hints: Quote your variables: "$SRC".
Stop on errors: set -e, or check the result of cp.
Print the success message only after cp has worked.
solution:
cat > /usr/local/bin/backup.sh <<'X'
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
SRC=$1
cp -r "$SRC" /backup/
echo "backup finished OK"
X

title: The tool a new shell cannot find
story: The command deploytool lives in /opt/tools/bin and needs APP_ENV=staging. A new login shell must be able to run it with no extra typing.
goals: Make `sh -lc deploytool` work.
Do it in a startup file, not by copying the tool.
hints: A login shell reads /etc/profile and then ~/.profile.
Put an export PATH line and an export APP_ENV line in /root/.profile.
Test with a new login shell: sh -lc deploytool
solution:
cat >> /root/.profile <<'X'
export PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools/bin
export APP_ENV=staging
X
sh -lc deploytool
